value.overview: The Black-cheeked Ant-Tanager (Driophlox atrimaxillaris) is a small, range-restricted songbird of the humid Pacific lowlands of Costa Rica. It has dark facial markings, olive-green upperparts, and reddish tones in the underparts, with males generally more strongly colored than females. The species is closely associated with dense forest and tangled vegetation, especially in the biologically rich Golfo Dulce region and on the Osa Peninsula.
value.classification: The Black-cheeked Ant-Tanager belongs to the tanager family Thraupidae. It was formerly placed in the genus Habia but is now treated in Driophlox.
value.identification: This ant-tanager is recognized by its compact body, fairly stout bill, dark cheek and ear-coverts, and contrasting reddish or rufous coloration on the breast and belly. The back is mainly olive-green, while the head and facial pattern appear darker. Females are generally duller than males. It can be confused with other ant-tanagers in Costa Rica, so its very restricted Pacific lowland range is an important identification clue.
value.rangeHabitat: The Black-cheeked Ant-Tanager is endemic to Costa Rica, where it occurs mainly in the humid southwestern Pacific region, particularly around the Golfo Dulce lowlands and the Osa Peninsula. It inhabits mature evergreen rainforest, forest edges, dense second growth, and thick understory near streams or other humid areas. Most records are from low elevations, generally below about 300 meters, although local elevational limits may vary. It is not normally found in the drier northern or central parts of the country.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica; it is not known to undertake regular long-distance migration. Movements are likely local and may follow changes in food availability or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Reliable detailed information on the breeding biology of the Black-cheeked Ant-Tanager is limited. Breeding is believed to occur during the wetter part of the year, when food is more abundant in southwestern Costa Rica. Like related ant-tanagers, it probably nests in dense vegetation and may breed cooperatively or in small social groups, but nest placement, clutch size, incubation, and parental care should be treated as incompletely documented.
value.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on insects and other small invertebrates, along with fruit and possibly small seeds. It searches through dense understory vegetation, foliage, vines, and shaded forest edges. It may forage singly, in pairs, or in small groups, and can sometimes join mixed-species feeding flocks. Despite its common name, it is not dependent solely on army-ant swarms.
value.behavior: The Black-cheeked Ant-Tanager is an active, relatively secretive bird of thick vegetation. It usually keeps to the understory and lower middle levels of humid forest, moving through foliage while giving short calls and searching for prey. Social behavior may include pair or family groups and associations with other forest birds. Its restricted distribution makes local habitat conditions especially important to its daily movements and survival.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is considered to be declining, primarily because of habitat loss, degradation, and fragmentation within its limited range.
conservation.threats: Important threats include clearing of lowland rainforest for agriculture, pasture, roads, settlements, and tourism infrastructure; fragmentation of remaining forest; degradation of forest edges and understory; and the effects of a very small geographic range. Climate change may add further pressure by altering humid lowland habitats and increasing extreme weather risks.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore humid lowland forest in the Golfo Dulce region and on the Osa Peninsula. Support conservation areas, wildlife corridors, and locally managed reforestation using native plants. Avoid clearing forest and dense streamside vegetation, promote bird-friendly farming and tourism practices, and report sightings through established Costa Rican bird-monitoring or biodiversity-recording programs.
